summary: Updates the IANA rules for allocating Diameter command codes from RFC 3588, so that the allocation policy makes sense for how Diameter is extended. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 6733.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5719 changes how IANA assigns Diameter command codes. Different ranges now have different rules for standard, vendor-specific, and experimental commands.

questions: how are diameter command codes allocated
what are the diameter vendor-specific code values
what changed in the diameter command allocation policy
subtitle: Allocation policies for Diameter command code ranges.

tldr.problem: The Diameter command allocation rule led some standards organizations to reuse existing commands instead of requesting new command codes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5719 divides command codes into ranges for RADIUS compatibility, IETF-reviewed standard commands, vendor-specific commands, and experiments.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5719 updates RFC 3588 and was obsoleted by RFC 6733.

today: RFC 5719 was obsoleted by RFC 6733 and updates RFC 3588, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why the Allocation Policy Changed
sections.content: The Diameter base specification allows extensions through new applications and commands. RFC 3588 required IETF consensus for new commands, while new applications did not require it. The RFC says some organizations responded by overloading existing commands, which in some cases caused interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Some groups reused existing commands rather than request a new code. The RFC says this approach caused interoperability problems in some cases.

sections.title: Command Code Ranges
sections.content: Values 0 through 255 are reserved for RADIUS backward compatibility. Values 256 through 8,388,607 are for standard commands allocated by IETF Review. Values 8,388,608 through 16,777,213 are for vendor-specific commands allocated First Come, First Served. Values 16,777,214 and 16,777,215 are reserved for experimental commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The code space is split into ranges for compatibility, standard commands, vendor-specific commands, and experiments. Each range follows its own allocation rule.

sections.title: Security and External Specifications
sections.content: The RFC says the process change itself raises no security concerns. It notes that organizations outside the IETF may use different security review criteria when producing specifications for vendor-specific codes. Those organizations are responsible for the quality of their specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Different organizations may review security in different ways. The RFC makes each organization responsible for the quality of its specifications.
